abstract: E-commerce UI UX design shapes the user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) of a retail business beyond the checkout funnel: site search, merchandising, loyalty, omnichannel journeys and seller tools. Our engagements for retailers, direct-to-consumer (DTC) brands, marketplaces and business-to-business (B2B) sellers run 4–8 weeks, cost $25,000–$60,000, and ship on Shopify, Adobe Commerce or Salesforce Commerce Cloud.

sections.h2: What is e-commerce UI UX design?
sections.answer: E-commerce UI UX design is the design of every customer-facing and staff-facing screen a retail business runs, from site search and loyalty accounts to the seller dashboard of a marketplace. The work connects the online store with physical stores and customer service, so shoppers meet 1 brand in every channel.
sections.body: Merchandisers manage search rules, store associates fulfil buy online, pick up in store (BOPIS) orders, and marketplace sellers manage payouts, each in a different tool. Conversion work on product listing pages, product detail pages and checkout belongs to our e-commerce UX design services; this page covers the wider commerce operation around that funnel.

sections.h2: Which commerce experiences do we design beyond checkout?
sections.answer: We design 6 types of e-commerce products: site search and navigation, merchandising tools, loyalty and account areas, omnichannel journeys, marketplace seller dashboards and B2B commerce portals.

items.title: Site search and navigation.
items.body: Autocomplete and zero-result pages turn vague queries into products, for example typo-tolerant suggestions grouped by category and brand.

items.title: Merchandising tools.
items.body: Merchandisers pin, boost and bury products, for example a rule editor that previews the first 24 results.

items.title: Loyalty and account areas.
items.body: Members check points, tiers and order history, for example a tier-progress card showing points left before free shipping.

items.title: Omnichannel journeys.
items.body: Shoppers move between app, website and store, for example BOPIS order status and returns started online.

items.title: Marketplace seller dashboards.
items.body: Third-party sellers manage listings, stock and payouts, for example a bulk listing upload with row-level errors.

items.title: B2B commerce portals.
items.body: Trade buyers order against negotiated prices, for example quick order by stock keeping unit (SKU) and purchase-order approval.

sections.h2: What UX challenges are specific to e-commerce?
sections.answer: 4 UX challenges are specific to e-commerce: search queries in shopper language, catalogue data quality, channel inconsistency and the needs of 2-sided marketplaces.

items.title: Search queries in shopper language
items.body: Shoppers type "red dress for a wedding" while the catalogue uses internal names, so search design depends on synonyms and zero-result pages.

items.title: Catalogue data quality
items.body: Missing attributes and inconsistent sizes break filters, so designers specify the attributes each category requires.

items.title: Channel inconsistency
items.body: Prices, stock and points differ between app, website and store when systems disagree, so screens show when stock data was updated.

items.title: Two-sided marketplace needs
items.body: Sellers want fewer listing fields and shoppers want complete product information, so research covers both sides together.

sections.h2: How does our e-commerce UI UX design process work?
sections.answer: Our commerce design process takes 4–8 weeks (20–40 working days) and runs in 5 steps, from the platform and catalogue review to the platform-ready handover.

items.title: Platform and catalogue review (3–5 days)
items.body: We review the platform, for example BigCommerce, the search engine such as Algolia, and the product information management (PIM) data behind filters.

items.title: Shopper and staff research (4–8 days)
items.body: We analyse site search logs for zero-result queries and interview shoppers plus merchandisers, store associates or sellers.

items.title: Journey and tool design (8–15 days)
items.body: Designers produce search, loyalty or seller screens as a Figma prototype, reusing platform components where the theme supports them.

items.title: Testing with shoppers and staff (3–7 days)
items.body: 5 shoppers per round test search tasks, and 3–5 staff users test merchandising or seller tasks with real catalogue data.

items.title: Platform-ready handover (2–5 days)
items.body: Developers receive Figma files mapped to Shopify sections or Salesforce Commerce Cloud components.

sections.h2: E-commerce UX vs content website UX
sections.answer: E-commerce UX designs revenue journeys that cross channels and staff tools; general product UX designs tasks inside 1 application. Catalogue data, promotions and payment rules shape almost every commerce screen.

sections.h2: How much does e-commerce UI UX design cost?
sections.answer: Commerce design work costs $25,000–$60,000 for a 4–8 week research and design sprint. The price depends on 4 factors: the platform's theme limits, the number of channels, the user groups beyond shoppers and catalogue data quality.
sections.body: A site search and zero-result redesign for a Shopify store with 1 catalogue sits near $25,000. A marketplace with a shopper app, seller dashboard and loyalty program across 3 channels sits near $60,000.

sections.h2: Which payment, accessibility and review rules shape e-commerce UX?
sections.answer: 5 standards and regulations shape e-commerce UX:
items: PCI DSS v4.0: requirement 6.4.3 makes teams authorise every script on payment pages, so designers keep third-party widgets out of the payment step.
WCAG 2.2 level AA: product images need alt text, filters need keyboard access and add-to-cart buttons need targets of at least 24×24 CSS pixels.
ADA Title III: US courts apply the ADA to online stores, so fixes go into templates instead of an overlay widget.
California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR): cookie banners and loyalty sign-up consent need choices with equal visual weight.

Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (16 CFR Part 465): fake reviews and review suppression are banned, so review displays show every star rating and label incentivised reviews.

sections.answer: These answers cover the 5 questions retail and marketplace teams ask most about commerce design beyond checkout.

faqs.q: Do you design marketplace seller dashboards?
faqs.a: Yes. Seller dashboard design covers onboarding, bulk listing upload, stock, orders, returns and payouts, and each flow is tested with 3–5 real sellers before development.

faqs.q: Does commerce design work include site search?
faqs.a: Yes. Site search design covers autocomplete, ranking rules, results filters and zero-result pages, with the top 100 queries from site search logs used as test material.

faqs.q: Can a Shopify store support a custom loyalty program design?
faqs.a: Yes. Shopify loyalty apps such as Smile.io and Yotpo expose theme blocks and APIs, so a custom points and tiers design ships without a headless rebuild.

faqs.q: Is B2B commerce design different from retail store design?
faqs.a: Yes. B2B buyers order against negotiated prices, credit terms and approval limits, so B2B portals need quick order by SKU, saved lists, purchase-order approval and invoice history instead of promotional banners.

faqs.q: How long does an e-commerce design project take?
faqs.a: An e-commerce design project takes 4–8 weeks, which equals 20–40 working days. A multi-brand storefront with a shared design system takes 8–16 weeks and costs $60,000–$180,000.
